text:
kyle: trying to repro a perf regression in kvcache kernel selection. nsys captures are massive and noisy for our multi-GPU runs. anyone with a compact capture recipe (trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt + sampling + duration) and tips for focusing on the KV hotpath? also seeing weird osrt sampling bias lately :/

anika: short checklist that usually helps:
- warm GPU w/ a few requests outside capture to stabilize kernels
- bracket the exact window you care about (short) — avoid full-run captures
- prefer sampling over full trace when possible to keep qdrep size down
- include nvtx markers around cache lookup / dispatch so you can filter in post

cj: +1. sample command we use (adapt per workload):
```bash
nsys profile -o kvcache_short --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --sample=cpu --sample-rate=1000 --duration=6s 
  --capture-range=pid:12345:12351 
  --force-overwrite
```
notes:
- --trace=osrt gives host-side scheduling info which is useful for batching heuristics
- --sample=cpu (or --sample=all depending on version) keeps kernel counts but reduces event noise

kyle: cj — how reliable is --capture-range=pid? we run many services on the node and sometimes the pid shifts between warmup and capture.

anika: if pid is flaky, use nvtx brackets instead. wrap the sequence like:
```python
with nvtx_range("kvcache:batch-serve"):
    serve_batch(...)
```
then `nsys` -> UI filter by NVTX name. bracketing + short duration is the most bulletproof.

sam: for multi-gpu thing, also:
- pin processes to GPUs (CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES / affinity) so timeline lines map cleanly
- reduce concurrency so the sampling window isn't spread thin across lots of tiny kernels

kyle: anyone seen osrt sampling show host-side threads as the top flame even though GPU kernels are heavy? that was confusing in last trace.

anika: yes. common causes:
- capture included warmup, and osrt samples host spinning/waiting threads more often
- sampling rate too low -> misses short GPU kernels, so host work looks dominant
fixes: bracket warmup, raise sample-rate briefly (if qdrep size allows), or do a very short high-rate capture focused on the hot request.

cj: extra tricks:
- use `nsys export` to slice qdrep to only the NVTX ranges you care about before exporting timelines
- if file still large, run `nsys stats` to get kernel aggregate numbers without full UI load
- try `--trace=cuda,osrt` only (drop nvtx) if you only need kernel timings and want smaller files; add nvtx back if you need filtering by logical batches

perf-bot: automated hint: uploaded preproc summary to S3 at s3://redwood-perf/kvcache/3772409876/summary.json :eyes:

kyle: awesome, will try bracket + nvtx + short high-rate sample. one more — any guidance on sample-rate vs duration tradeoff? we need to keep qdrep < ~200MB for CI artifact limits.

anika: heuristics:
- if qdrep size matters, prefer 3–6s at 1kHz and nvtx brackets (small, high-signal window)
- for very short kernels (<200us) you might need >2kHz but shorten to 1–2s capture to limit size
- if you can reproduce request deterministically, prefer multiple short captures over one long one (post-aggregate)

cj: final quick checklist before you run:
- isolate load (no other noisy services)
- set CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES and cpu affinity
- add NVTX ranges for 'kvcache:lookup' and 'kvcache:commit'
- warmup out of capture for ~10s
- run 3 short captures with slightly different sample-rate (1k/2k)

kyle: perfect, thanks. i'll post the qdrep links if the regression reproduces. :thumbsup:
